newsitem.title: ZIMBABWE: Britain pledges aid for Africa peace efforts.
newsitem.headline: Britain pledges aid for Africa peace efforts.

text.p: Britain's Prince Andrew witnessed a landmark joint military exercise by eight southern African nations in Zimbabwe on Thursday and pledged his country's support for more such programmes aimed at enhancing Africa's peacekeeping capabilities.
Speaking at the end of a three-hour drill in Zimbabwe's eastern district of Nyanga, the prince called on participants to build on the success of the 20-day military exercise ending on April 20.

Some 1,100 troops from Lesotho, Malawi, Mozambique, Namibia, South Africa, Swaziland, Tanzania and Zimbabwe -- all Commonwealth members -- are taking part in the exercise, the first of its kind in Africa aimed at honing peacekeeping skills.
The exercise is partly funded by Britain.
Prince Andrew was invited by Mugabe to witness the exercise, code-named Blue Hungwe (Fish Eagle), which is jointly run by London's Zimbabwe-based British Military Advisory and Training Team (BMATT).

On Thursday, the prince and Mugabe drove through dusty mountainous roads, and sat for 30 minutes under a blazing African sun following the drill on how some African troops would help restore peace and save lives in a country torn by civil war among rival ethnic groups.
The prince commended the training effort, saying it was relevant as some 16 African countries were currently contributing troops to United Nations peacekeeping efforts around the world.
"Britain is prepared to sponsor joint military exercises to enhance Africa's peacekeeping capabilities," he said.
Mugabe called on southern African states to stage the joint exercises -- based on U.N. tactics and techniques of international peacekeeping -- annually and on a rotational basis.
This approach, he said, would help the region to build a common military culture, which was crucial in maintaining peace and stability.

"Cooperation and co-existence has become extremely important because the problems being faced have become so transnational that no one nation can claim to have the ability and resources to deal with them in isolation," Mugabe said.
